abstract: The cerebral cortex acquires its neuronal diversity through successive waves of neurogenesis. How molecular differences among early progenitors relate to their neuronal output remains unclear. Here, we identify a molecular program in early SOX9-high radial glia (S9RGs) that links progenitor maintenance with the regulation of genes associated with neuronal identity. Combining transcriptional and chromatin profiling with in vivo perturbations, we identify a program involving extracellular signaling, cell-cycle regulation, progenitor maintenance, and neurogenesis. We show that SOX9 regulates part of this program, including receptors that contribute to progenitor maintenance, while Notch acts upstream of Sox9 and reproduces several transcriptional and chromatin features of S9RGs. S9RGs express selected later-stage radial glial features and show distinct chromatin accessibility patterns at genes involved in progenitor maintenance, neurogenesis, and neuronal identity. Notch activation reproduces part of these changes, including differences at genes associated with lower- and upper-layer neuronal specification. Interestingly, S9RGs, which preferentially generate upper-layer neurons, share molecular features with the highly proliferative RG population in ferrets and with human outer RGs (oRGs) from cortical organoids, despite their different positions within the developing cortex. Together, our findings suggest that molecular differences among early radial glia could influence both how long they remain as progenitors and the neuronal identities they subsequently generate.
